q: Change the following sentence into Indirect Speech: He said, "I am reading a novel."
o: He said that he is reading a novel.
He said that I was reading a novel.
He told that he was reading a novel.
He said that he was reading a novel.
e: When the reporting verb ("said") is in the past tense, Present Continuous ("am reading") backshifts to Past Continuous ("was reading"), and first-person "I" changes to third-person "he". "Told" requires an object and cannot be used without one.

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: She said to me, "I have completed my homework."
o: She told me that she has completed her homework.
She said to me that she completed her homework.
She asked me that she had completed her homework.
She told me that she had completed her homework.
e: "Said to" changes to "told" before an object ("me"). Present Perfect ("have completed") shifts to Past Perfect ("had completed"), and possessive "my" changes to "her" according to the subject "She".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The teacher said, "The Earth revolves around the Sun."
o: The teacher said that the Earth revolved around the Sun.
The teacher said that the Earth had revolved around the Sun.
The teacher told that the Earth is revolving around the Sun.
The teacher said that the Earth revolves around the Sun.
e: Universal truths, scientific facts, and proverbs retain their Present Simple tense in Indirect Speech even when the reporting verb is in the past tense. Hence, "revolves" remains unchanged.

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: Riya says, "I like classical music."
o: Riya says that she liked classical music.
Riya tells that she liked classical music.
Riya said that she likes classical music.
Riya says that she likes classical music.
e: When the reporting verb is in the Present ("says") or Future tense, the tense of the reported speech does NOT change. Only the pronoun ("I" → "she") and verb agreement ("like" → "likes") adjust.

q: Change into Indirect Speech: Mohan said, "I will visit Delhi tomorrow."
o: Mohan said that he would visit Delhi tomorrow.
Mohan said that he will visit Delhi the next day.
Mohan said that he would visit Delhi the next day.
Mohan said that he should visit Delhi the next day.
e: With a past reporting verb, "will" backshifts to "would", "I" changes to "he", and the time adverb "tomorrow" changes to "the next day" (or "the following day").

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: He said to her, "Are you coming to the party?"
o: He asked her that she was coming to the party.
He told her if she was coming to the party.
He asked her whether was she coming to the party.
He asked her if she was coming to the party.
e: Yes/No questions use "if" or "whether" (never "that") as the conjunction and change "said to" to "asked". Crucially, the word order becomes assertive (subject before verb: "she was coming", not "was she coming").

q: Change into Indirect Speech: She said to me, "Where do you live?"
o: She asked me where did I live.
She inquired me where I live.
She asked me that where I lived.
She asked me where I lived.
e: In Wh-questions, the Wh-word itself acts as the conjunction (no "that" or "if"). Auxiliary "do" is dropped, Present Simple backshifts to Past Simple ("lived"), and assertive order ("I lived") is maintained.

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: The old man said to the boy, "Please help me cross the road."
o: The old man ordered the boy to help him cross the road.
The old man asked the boy please to help him cross the road.
The old man requested the boy that he should help him cross the road.
The old man requested the boy to help him cross the road.
e: The word "Please" signals a request, so "said to" becomes "requested", "please" is dropped, and the imperative verb is introduced with the to-infinitive ("to help"). Pronoun "me" shifts to "him".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The captain said to the soldiers, "March forward."
o: The captain requested the soldiers to march forward.
The captain advised the soldiers marching forward.
The captain told the soldiers that march forward.
The captain commanded the soldiers to march forward.
e: A military command uses reporting verbs like "commanded" or "ordered", followed by object + to-infinitive ("to march forward").

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: My father said to me, "Do not waste your time."
o: My father advised me to not waste my time.
My father ordered me that do not waste my time.
My father forbade me not to waste my time.
My father advised me not to waste my time.
e: Negative imperatives ("Do not + V1") change into "not to + V1" after "advised/ordered/warned". Note that "forbade" is already negative, so "forbade me not to" is a double negative error ("forbade me to waste" would be correct).

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The boys said, "Hurrah! We have won the match."
o: The boys exclaimed with joy that they had won the match.
The boys said with joy that they have won the match.
The boys exclaimed happily that we had won the match.
The boys shouted with sorrow that they had won the match.
e: "Hurrah!" expresses joy, so "said" becomes "exclaimed with joy", the interjection is omitted, "that" is added, "we" becomes "they", and Present Perfect ("have won") shifts to Past Perfect ("had won").

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: She said to me, "May God bless you!"
o: She prayed that God might bless me.
She wished me that God may bless me.
She told me that God might bless you.
She exclaimed that God might bless me.
e: Optative sentences invoking God use "prayed" (without a direct object before "that"), "may" backshifts to "might", and second-person "you" changes to "me" according to the listener.

q: Change into Indirect Speech: Anil said, "I can solve this puzzle easily."
o: Anil said that he can solve that puzzle easily.
Anil told that he could solve that puzzle easily.
Anil said that he could solve this puzzle easily.
Anil said that he could solve that puzzle easily.
e: Under a past reporting verb, modal "can" backshifts to "could" and demonstrative "this" changes to "that".

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: Grandfather said, "Honesty is the best policy."
o: Grandfather said that honesty was the best policy.
Grandfather said that honesty has been the best policy.
Grandfather told that honesty is the best policy.
Grandfather said that honesty is the best policy.
e: Proverbs and timeless moral maxims do not undergo tense backshift in Indirect Speech; "is" stays in the Present Simple.

q: Change into Direct Speech: He told me that he was very tired.
o: He said to me, "He is very tired."
He asked me, "Am I very tired?"
He said to me, "I was very tired."
He said to me, "I am very tired."
e: Reversing Indirect to Direct: "told me" reverts to "said to me", third-person "he" referring to the speaker reverts to "I", and Past Simple "was" reverts to Present Simple "am".

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: She said, "I bought a new laptop yesterday."
o: She said that she bought a new laptop the previous day.
She said that she had bought a new laptop yesterday.
She said that she had bought a new laptop the previous day.
She said that she has bought a new laptop the day before.
e: Past Simple ("bought") backshifts to Past Perfect ("had bought"), and "yesterday" changes to "the previous day" or "the day before".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: They said, "We were playing cricket when it began to rain."
o: They said that they were playing cricket when it began to rain.
They said that they had been playing cricket when it had begun to rain.
They said that they had been playing cricket when it began to rain.
They told that they were playing cricket when it had begun to rain.
e: Past Continuous ("were playing") shifts to Past Perfect Continuous ("had been playing"), while a Past Simple verb in a time clause introduced by "when/while" typically remains in Past Simple ("began") to preserve temporal clarity.

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: The policeman said to the driver, "Why did you jump the red light?"
o: The policeman asked the driver why did he jump the red light.
The policeman asked the driver why he jumped the red light.
The policeman asked the driver why he had jumped the red light.
The policeman inquired the driver why had he jumped the red light.
e: In Wh-questions, "did + V1" (Past Simple) converts to Past Perfect ("had + V3" = "had jumped") in assertive subject-verb order ("he had jumped").

q: Change into Indirect Speech: Priya said to her friends, "Let us go for a picnic this Sunday."
o: Priya ordered her friends to go for a picnic that Sunday.
Priya suggested her friends that we should go for a picnic this Sunday.
Priya proposed to her friends that they should go for a picnic that Sunday.
Priya requested her friends to let them go for a picnic that Sunday.
e: "Let us" expressing a proposal/suggestion changes to "proposed to / suggested to" + object + "that they/we should + V1", and "this" changes to "that". Note that "proposed" and "suggested" MUST take "to" before a personal object.

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: The student said to the teacher, "Let me go home early today."
o: The student proposed to the teacher that he should go home early that day.
The student ordered the teacher to allow him going home early today.
The student requested the teacher to let him go home early that day.
The student requested the teacher that he may go home early that day.
e: When "Let me/him/her" seeks permission (not a joint proposal), "said to" becomes "requested/asked", followed by "to let + pronoun + V1" (or "that he might be allowed to go"), and "today" becomes "that day".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: He said, "What a beautiful painting this is!"
o: He exclaimed that what a beautiful painting that was.
He said that this was a very beautiful painting.
He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful painting.
He exclaimed with wonder that how beautiful that painting was.
e: In exclamatory sentences beginning with "What a/an + adj + noun", "What" is replaced by "very" (or "great" before a noun alone), and the sentence takes assertive order: "He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful painting."

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: The woman said, "Alas! I have lost my only son."
o: The woman exclaimed with sorrow that she had lost her only son.
The woman exclaimed with grief that she has lost her only son.
The woman said sadly that I had lost my only son.
The woman cried with regret that she lost her only son.
e: "Alas!" conveys deep grief/sorrow, so "said" becomes "exclaimed with sorrow/grief", "I/my" become "she/her", and "have lost" backshifts to "had lost".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: He said, "Good-bye, my friends!"
o: He wished his friends good-bye.
He told his friends good-bye.
He bade his friends good-bye.
He greeted his friends good-bye.
e: For parting expressions like "Good-bye", "Farewell", or "Good night", the standard reporting verb in Indirect Speech is "bade" (past tense of "bid"), whereas "wished" is used for "Good morning/evening".

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: He said, "I must finish this report tonight."
o: He said that he must finish that report tonight.
He said that he has to finish that report that night.
He said that he had to finish that report that night.
He said that he must have finished that report that night.
e: When "must" expresses a present/immediate personal necessity or obligation, it changes to "had to" in Indirect Speech, and "this/tonight" shift to "that/that night". (Permanent rules/prohibitions retain "must".)

q: Change into Indirect Speech: She said to me, "You ought to respect your elders."
o: She told me that I had to respect my elders.
She told me that I would respect my elders.
She told me that I ought to respect my elders.
She advised me that you ought to respect your elders.
e: Past-form and defective modals such as "ought to", "would", "should", "could", "might", and "used to" remain unchanged in Indirect Speech. Only pronouns ("you/your" → "I/my") change.

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: He said, "If it rains, I will cancel the trip."
o: He said that if it rains, he would cancel the trip.
He said that if it had rained, he would have cancelled the trip.
He said that if it rained, he would cancel the trip.
He said that if it rained, he will cancel the trip.
e: A Type-1 real conditional ("If + Present Simple, will + V1") backshifts cleanly to a Type-2 pattern ("If + Past Simple, would + V1") when reported in the past.

q: Change into Indirect Speech: My mother said to me, "Will you take tea or coffee?"
o: My mother asked me if would I take tea or coffee.
My mother told me whether I would take tea or coffee.
My mother asked me whether I would take tea or coffee.
My mother asked me that I would take tea or coffee.
e: When a choice is explicitly presented with "or", "whether" is preferred over "if", and "will" shifts to "would" in assertive word order ("I would take").

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: The speaker said, "Ladies and gentlemen, I thank you for your support."
o: The speaker said to ladies and gentlemen that he thanked them for their support.
The speaker exclaimed to ladies and gentlemen that he thanked them for their support.
Addressing the audience as ladies and gentlemen, the speaker thanked them for their support.
The speaker told ladies and gentlemen that I thank you for your support.
e: Vocative terms of address ("Ladies and gentlemen", "Friends", "Comrades") are naturally rendered using the participial phrase "Addressing them/the audience as ...", followed by the reported clause.

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The coach said to the player, "Bravo! You have played brilliantly."
o: The coach applauded the player, saying that he had played brilliantly.
The coach exclaimed with joy to the player that he has played brilliantly.
The coach told the player bravo that he had played brilliantly.
The coach praised the player that you had played brilliantly.
e: "Bravo!" expresses applause/praise and is idiomatically reported using "applauded [object], saying that ..." with standard tense backshift ("have played" → "had played").

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: She said to me, "Could you please lend me your pen?"
o: She asked me if I could please lend her my pen.
She requested me to lend her my pen.
She ordered me to lend her my pen.
She inquired whether I lent her my pen.
e: Sentences beginning with "Could you please..." or "Would you mind..." are functionally polite requests rather than information questions; they are best converted using "requested + object + to-infinitive".

q: Change into Direct Speech: He asked me if I knew where his sister lived.
o: He said to me, "Do you know where my sister lives?"
He said to me, "Did you know where my sister lived?"
He said to me, "Do you know where his sister lives?"
He said to me, "Do you knew where my sister lives?"
e: Reversing Past Simple "knew" and "lived" gives Present Simple "Do you know" and "lives"; "I" reverts to "you" and "his" reverts to "my".

q: Convert into Direct Speech: The doctor advised the patient not to eat fried food.
o: The doctor said to the patient, "Never you eat fried food."
The doctor said to the patient, "Do not eat fried food."
The doctor said to the patient, "You should not have eaten fried food."
The doctor asked the patient, "Why do you eat fried food?"
e: "Advised [object] not to + V1" directly corresponds to the negative imperative "Do not + V1" in Direct Speech.

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The history teacher said, "India gained independence in 1947."
o: The history teacher said that India had gained independence in 1947.
The history teacher said that India gained independence in 1947.
The history teacher said that India gains independence in 1947.
The history teacher told that India gained independence in 1947.
e: Established historical facts with fixed past dates do NOT backshift from Past Simple to Past Perfect in Indirect Speech; "gained" remains Past Simple.

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: The librarian said to the students, "Do not make a noise here."
o: The librarian forbade the students not to make a noise there.
The librarian forbade the students to make a noise there.
The librarian forbade the students from making a noise here.
The librarian ordered the students to not make a noise here.
e: "Forbade" already carries negative force ("ordered not to"), so it is followed directly by "to + V1" (never "not to"), and "here" changes to "there".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The old king said, "O that I were young again!"
o: The old king exclaimed that he was young again.
The old king wished that he were young again.
The old king prayed that he might be young again.
The old king said that he had been young again.
e: Expressions of ardent unreal wishes ("O that...", "Would that...", "If only...") are reported with "wished that..." and retain the subjunctive "were" (or "had been" if past unreal).

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: He said, "If I were a bird, I would fly to the Himalayas."
o: He said that if he had been a bird, he would have flown to the Himalayas.
He said that if he were a bird, he would fly to the Himalayas.
He said that if he was a bird, he will fly to the Himalayas.
He wished that he would be a bird to fly to the Himalayas.
e: Improbable/unreal Type-2 conditionals ("If + were/V2, would + V1") and Type-3 conditionals remain UNCHANGED in tense during Indirect Speech conversion; only pronouns shift ("I" → "he").

q: Change into Indirect Speech: She said, "While I was cooking, my brother was watching television."
o: She said that while she had been cooking, her brother had been watching television.
She said that while she was cooking, her brother was watching television.
She said that while she cooked, her brother was watching television.
She told that while she was cooking, her brother watched television.
e: When two actions are shown occurring simultaneously in the past (joined by "while"), the Past Continuous verbs do NOT backshift to Past Perfect Continuous; only pronouns change ("I/my" → "she/her").

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: She said to me, "You have met him before, haven't you?"
o: She asked me if I had met him before, hadn't I.
She asked me whether I had met him before.
She told me that I had met him before, hadn't I.
She asked me that I had met him before.
e: In Indirect Speech, the question tag ("haven't you?") is completely dropped, and the entire sentence is reported as a regular Yes/No question using "asked + if/whether" with tense backshift ("have met" → "had met").

q: Change into Indirect Speech: She said, "You needn't wait for me today."
o: She told me that I didn't have to wait for her that day.
She told me that I hadn't needed to wait for her today.
She told me that I needn't wait for her today.
She ordered me not to wait for her that day.
e: "Needn't" expressing absence of immediate obligation changes to "didn't have to" (or "wouldn't have to" for future) in Indirect Speech, and "today" shifts to "that day".

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: The mathematician said, "Let ABC be an equilateral triangle."
o: The mathematician ordered that ABC be an equilateral triangle.
The mathematician supposed ABC to be an equilateral triangle.
The mathematician proposed that ABC should be an equilateral triangle.
The mathematician requested that ABC might be an equilateral triangle.
e: When "Let" introduces a mathematical or logical assumption/supposition (not a command or proposal), the reporting verb becomes "supposed" ("supposed ABC to be...").

q: Change into Indirect Speech: He said, "Let it rain ever so hard, I will attend the seminar."
o: He said that however hard it might rain, he would attend the seminar.
He proposed that it should rain hard so he could attend the seminar.
He ordered that it might rain hard while he attended the seminar.
He exclaimed that if it rained hard, he would attend the seminar.
e: "Let it..." conveying concession or indifference ("no matter how...") is converted using "however + adj/adv + subject + might + V1", followed by the main clause with "will" → "would".

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: He said to me, "I am leaving for Agra tonight. Will you come with me?"
o: He told me that he was leaving for Agra that night and asked if I would go with him.
He told me that he is leaving for Agra that night and asked if I will go with him.
He asked me that he was leaving for Agra that night and whether I would come with him.
He told me that he was leaving for Agra tonight and asked me to come with him.
e: Mixed sentences require separate appropriate reporting verbs joined by "and": "told me that..." for the assertive statement and "asked if..." for the question, with "come" shifting to "go" and "tonight" to "that night".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The officer said to the clerk, "Submit the file at once, or I shall suspend you."
o: The officer ordered the clerk to submit the file at once and threatened to suspend him if he failed to do so.
The officer requested the clerk to submit the file at once or he would suspend him.
The officer ordered the clerk that submit the file at once or he shall suspend him.
The officer told the clerk to submit the file at once and said I would suspend you.
e: An imperative followed by a threat ("or I shall...") is accurately reported by combining "ordered [object] to + V1" with "and threatened to..." (or "and warned him that he would suspend him if he did not").

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: I said to Rohan, "Have you read Hamlet?" He replied, "No."
o: I asked Rohan if he had read Hamlet and he replied that no.
I asked Rohan if he had read Hamlet and he replied in the negative.
I asked Rohan whether he read Hamlet and he denied it.
I inquired Rohan if he had read Hamlet and he said no.
e: Short responses "Yes" and "No" in dialogues are rendered as "replied in the affirmative" / "replied in the negative" (or "replied that he had / had not"), never "replied that yes/no".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: She said to him, "Congratulations! You have topped the university."
o: She told him congratulations that he had topped the university.
She congratulated him on having topped the university.
She exclaimed with congratulations that he topped the university.
She wished him congratulations for topping the university.
e: Expressions like "Thank you", "Congratulations", and "Sorry" turn directly into reporting verbs: "congratulated [object] on + gerund / saying that...". Never use "for" after "congratulate"—always "on".

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: He said to me, "It is high time you started preparing seriously."
o: He told me that it was high time I had started preparing seriously.
He told me that it was high time I started preparing seriously.
He told me that it is high time I start preparing seriously.
He advised me that it was high time you started preparing seriously.
e: After "It is time / It is high time", the unreal past verb ("started") does NOT backshift to Past Perfect in Indirect Speech; only the main verb "is" becomes "was" and "you" becomes "I".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: Looking at the ruined crops, the farmer said, "What a terrible disaster!"
o: Looking at the ruined crops, the farmer exclaimed that it was a terrible disaster.
Looking at the ruined crops, the farmer asked what a terrible disaster it was.
Looking at the ruined crops, the farmer said that what a terrible disaster.
Looking at the ruined crops, the farmer exclaimed with joy that it was a terrible disaster.
e: Verbless exclamatory phrases ("What a terrible disaster!") are expanded into full assertive clauses ("it was a terrible disaster") introduced by "exclaimed that".

q: Convert into Direct Speech: He swore by God that he had not stolen the jewels.
o: He said, "By God, I did not steal the jewels."
He said, "I swear by God that he had not stolen the jewels."
He said, "By God, I have not been stealing the jewels."
He said, "God knows I will not steal the jewels."
e: "Swore by God" reverses to the oath "By God," in Direct Speech; Past Perfect "had not stolen" reverses to Past Simple "did not steal" (or Present Perfect "have not stolen"), and "he" reverts to "I".

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The editor of the newspaper wrote, "We strongly condemn this policy."
o: The editor of the newspaper wrote that they strongly condemned that policy.
The editor of the newspaper wrote that it strongly condemned that policy.
The editor of the newspaper wrote that he strongly condemns this policy.
The editor of the newspaper wrote that we strongly condemned that policy.
e: When a newspaper, magazine, or institution uses the "editorial we", "we" changes to singular "it" (representing the publication/institution) in Indirect Speech—a classic UP TGT English grammar rule.

q: Convert into Direct Speech: The soldiers exclaimed with grief that their brave commander was no more and prayed that his soul might rest in peace.
o: The soldiers said, "Alas! Our brave commander is no more. May his soul rest in peace!"
The soldiers said, "Hurrah! Our brave commander was no more. May his soul rest in peace!"
The soldiers said, "Alas! Their brave commander is no more. Might his soul rest in peace!"
The soldiers said, "Oh! Our brave commander had been no more. Let his soul rest in peace!"
e: "Exclaimed with grief" reverses to "Alas!", "their/was" revert to "Our/is", and "prayed that his soul might rest in peace" reverts to the optative "May his soul rest in peace!".
